div.b: Why scale-in is the fast direction

div.div: Stopping a task is a signal plus a drain. Nothing has to be downloaded, started or proved healthy, so the whole move finishes in seconds. Plan your capacity around the slow direction, not this one.

div.div: If the autoscaler is switched on, it will undo you

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 634px; height: 1px; padding-top: 730px; margin-left: 44px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 13px; font-family: Helvetica; color: #000000; line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;
div.div: You set five tasks by hand. The service is idle, so AlarmLow fires fifteen minutes later and walks the count back: five, four, three, and on down to min_capacity. Nothing is broken; two controllers simply disagree about who owns the number.

div.b: The ALB drains before ECS stops

div.span: - Four targets are deregistered and their in-flight requests are allowed to finish. That is why nobody sees an error while the service shrinks.

div.b: Before you set a CPU target

div.div: A single-threaded app on 0.25 vCPU alternates between idle and fully busy, so its average settles near 50 % however hard you push it. Pick a target below that plateau, or the high alarm will never fire. This lab uses 30 % for exactly that reason, and measuring your own plateau first is the habit worth taking away.
